note_a: Rust offers several constructs for repetition. An infinite loop is introduced with the `loop` keyword followed by a block. Iteration can be cut short with `break;`, which forcibly exits the current loop. To skip the rest of the current iteration and move on to the next, `continue;` is used. The behavior of `continue;` is to abandon the remainder of the loop body and proceed with the next iteration rather than terminate the loop.
note_b: Rust also supports more structured looping patterns. A value can be returned out of a `loop` so that it is usable after the loop ends by placing an expression after `break`, such as `break counter * 2;`. When loops are nested, an inner `break` or `continue` can target a specific outer loop by attaching a labelled name with a leading apostrophe, for example `'outer: loop { … break 'outer; }`. A `while` loop runs while its condition holds, so a countdown that loops three times can be written as `let mut count = 3; while count != 0 { … count -= 1; }`. For running code a known number of times over a collection, a `for` loop with a range is generally preferred to `while`.

note_a: Compound types in Rust group multiple values into a single type. Rust's primitive compound types are the tuple and the array. note_a: Rust's ownership model rests on three rules: each value has an owner, there can be only one owner at a time, and when the owner goes out of scope the value is dropped. String literals are convenient but unsuitable in some situations because they are immutable and because not every string value can be known when the code is written, such as data taken from user input. For those cases Rust provides the `String` type, which manages data allocated on the heap and can store text whose size is unknown at compile time. A `String` value is internally three pieces of data stored on the stack — a pointer to the heap-allocated contents, a length, and a capacity — while the actual bytes live on the heap.
note_b: Because a `String`'s contents live on the heap, ownership interacts in subtle ways with assignment. When `let s2 = s1;` is written for a `String`, only the stack data (pointer, length, and capacity) is copied; the heap data is not. To prevent a double-free, Rust invalidates the original variable, and this is called a *move* rather than a shallow copy. Attempting to use `s1` after `let s2 = s1;` therefore produces a compile-time error. The explicit way to duplicate the heap data is `s1.clone()`, but this should be a red flag because cloning can be expensive and signals that nontrivial work is happening.

note_a: References allow a value to be used without taking ownership of it. A reference is created with an ampersand, as in `calculate_length(&s1)`, and the action of creating one is called *borrowing*. Unlike an arbitrary pointer, a Rust reference is guaranteed to point to a valid value of a particular type for the life of the reference. By default a borrow is read-only; mutation through a reference is not possible unless the reference is explicitly mutable. The compiler enforces two rules of references: at any moment, code can hold either one mutable reference or any number of immutable references, and references must always be valid.
note_b: Mutable references carry additional restrictions. If code holds a mutable reference to a value, it cannot simultaneously hold any other reference, mutable or immutable, to that same value. The benefit of this restriction is that Rust can prevent data races at compile time. A data race needs three conditions: two or more pointers accessing the same data simultaneously, at least one of them writing, and no mechanism synchronizing the accesses. Where multiple mutable references are needed, the workaround is to use curly brackets to create non-overlapping scopes, since references go out of scope at the end of their block. Multiple immutable references are still allowed because read-only observers cannot affect each other, whereas a mutable reference could change the value out from under an immutable observer.

Rust's compiler guarantees that references will never be dangling: if code holds a reference to some data, the compiler ensures that the data will not go out of scope before the reference does. Like other references, a string slice borrows from the underlying string and obeys the same scoping rules.
